newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends firmer vs. mark, helped by pound.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends firmer vs. mark, helped by pound.

text.p: The dollar rose with the British pound against the German mark Friday as the pound recovered from a sell-off that followed a stunning victory by Britain's Labour Party in national elections.
The elections Thursday put an end to 18 years of Conservative rule in Britain.

Initially, the pound tumbled in Asia partly in reaction to the election and an editorial in London's The Times newspaper that said the new government "must create conditions for (an) immediate fall in the pound" to avoid economic damage.
The article also said taxes need to rise to counter the pressure for higher interest rates. A strong pound can hurt the economy by making British exports less competitive.
The pound fell against the marks but later bounced back and as the pound recovered it helped pull the dollar higher versus the German currency.
The dollar stood at 1.7293 marks in late New York trading, up from 1.7225 marks late on Thursday. The dollar rose marginally to 126.62 Japanese yen from 126.58 yen.
Against other currencies, the dollar edged up to 1.4710 Swiss francs from 1.4705 francs. But it fell to Canadian $1.3807 from C$1.3876.
Bob Lynch, a senior currency analyst at MMS International, said the pound's recovery against the mark "is supportive of dollar-mark but not overly so."

Other traders and analysts said gains in the stock and bond markets helped the dollar. The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 94.72 points, or 1.36 percent, to 7,071.20. The 30-year Treasury rose 15/32 higher to yield 6.88 percent, down from 6.92 percent on Thursday.
"Those are not reasons to go and sell the dollar," said David Durrant, a senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc., referring to the rally in stocks and bonds.
The government's April employment report sent mixed signals to the currency market.

The Labour Department said the economy created 142,000 jobs in April, a figure well below the 211,000 gain expected by Wall Street economists. The amount of jobs added in March was revised down to 139,000 from a previously reported 175,000.
Furthermore, the length of the average work week shrank to 34.6 hours in April from 34.9 hours in March, while average hourly earnings fell 1 cent in April to $12.14.
In contrast to the other data, the jobless rate fell to 4.9 percent in April, its lowest since a 4.8 percent rate in November of 1973. The unemployment rate in March stood at 5.2 percent.

"They saw moderate numbers, that's why they sold the dollar as the initial reaction," said Takanobu Igarashi, a senior economist at Sanwa Bank Ltd in New York. "But then they realised the unemployment rate was down to 4.9 percent ... and they bought the dollar back."
